newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britain moves to toughen rail regulation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britain moves to toughen rail regulation.

text.p: British regulators on Wednesday said they would consider modifying Railtrack Plc's licence to ensure timely completion of a 16 billion pound ($26.5 billion) infrastructure investment plan.
"It is now timely to introduce a greater measure of accountability," John Swift, the director of Britain's Office of Rail Regulation told a news conference in London.
Railtrack is responsible for maintaining Britain's rail track and stations and was privatised on year ago on Tuesday.

"I have commenced discussions with Railtrack to seek to agree with it an appropriate modification to its license which would meet public interest concerns without prejudicing its effective management of a properly directed capital investment programme," Swift said.
Railtrack unveiled a 16 billion pound plan in February aimed at an across-the-board revamp of Britain's rail network.
Swift hailed it as an important first step towards demonstrating Railtrack's commitment to planning and investment.
"However, there is more to be done and I am asking Railtrack, over the course of the year, to set out more detail on their plans in a number of important areas," he said.
"It is now timely to consider strengthening Railtrack's obligation to ensure delivery of those plans."
The regulators received backing from Britain's new Labour government, which said it would review options to toughen the regulation of privatised rail companies such as Railtrack.
"The regulation of the rail industry, and the sanctions available to the regulators, need to be strengthened," Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott said in a statement.
Prescott specifically pencilled in the need for a system which would guarantee effective spending of money which Railtrack receives each year.
Swift said he would be meeting government transport officials to discuss the issue further.
Railtrack had promised in February that it would invest 8.3 billion pounds on renewal and 5.7 billion pounds on day-to-day maintenance.

The company gave a strong message on Tuesday that it was sticking to its promise by announcing it would spend 1.0 billion pounds to upgrade 2,500 stations across Britain, many of them built in the early part of the century.
"We are getting on with the job and delivering our promises," Railtrack's chairman Sir Robert Horton said.

Swift also said his office would not hesitate in taking suitable measures against Railtrack if its performance fell below expectations, although he fell short of spelling out any sanctions against non-performance.

"I will take those measures which are in my view appropriate and proportionate to the delivery of a better railway. One will have to wait and see hypothetically what is the point at which non-delivery by Railtrack will bring greater or less sanctions from the regulator," Swift said.
If Railtrack disagrees with a proposed licensing change, it has the right to refer it to the Monopolies and Merger Commission. ($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
